mcqs.question: Per Conway's Law, why does an organization's communication structure end up mirrored in the system it builds, even without anyone designing for it?
options: Developers who need cross-team changes either wait on slow cross-team requests or build workarounds, and both responses shape the actual architecture over time
Conway's Law only applies to companies that explicitly plan their architecture around team structure
The effect is purely coincidental and has no identifiable mechanism
It only applies to organizations with more than 500 engineers
mcqs.explanation: The mechanism is concrete: cross-team dependencies are slower to resolve than in-team ones, so engineers minimize them or route around them with workarounds, and those everyday choices accumulate into an architecture that mirrors the org's communication paths. It applies regardless of explicit planning, has an identifiable causal mechanism (not coincidence), and isn't gated by company size.

mcqs.question: A "Pricing" capability is logically one clean bounded context, but two separate teams (Promotions and Catalog) each need to independently own and change parts of it. What is the expert-level recommendation?
options: Always keep Pricing as one service regardless of team structure, since domain purity should never be compromised

Split along the team seam (even if it makes the domain model less pure) or reorganize the teams to match the domain — either is legitimate, but a domain-pure boundary with no single owning team is not
Assign Pricing to whichever team is larger and let the other team file change requests
Merge Promotions and Catalog into a single team regardless of their other responsibilities
mcqs.explanation: The two legitimate fixes are splitting along the team boundary (accepting an imperfect domain model) or realigning the teams to match the domain — what's not viable is a domain-pure service with no single owning team, since that reliably produces coordination overhead. Never compromising purity ignores the real cost, assigning ownership by team size just recreates the coordination problem for the smaller team, and merging teams wholesale ignores their other responsibilities and isn't the general answer.

mcqs.question: In a growing organization with several active teams, the compare table suggests weighting which factor more heavily when choosing between Conway's-Law alignment and domain-model purity?
options: Domain-model purity, since it never needs to be revisited once designed
Neither — the two factors are always equally weighted regardless of context
Domain-model purity, since it directly determines team velocity
Conway's-Law alignment, since a slightly less pure model owned cleanly by one team beats a perfect model requiring multiple teams' agreement to change
mcqs.explanation: In an org with several active teams, autonomy tends to be the bigger velocity bottleneck, so a boundary that one team can own cleanly — even if not textbook-pure — usually outperforms a perfect domain model that needs cross-team sign-off. Purity does need revisiting as the org changes, purity doesn't itself determine velocity (alignment does more directly here), and the two factors aren't always equally weighted — context should shift the balance.

mcqs.question: A team designs a domain-pure "Pricing" service split exactly along bounded-context lines, but two other teams need to change it weekly and every release requires negotiating whose change merges first. What does this scenario illustrate?
options: That the domain model must be wrong, since a correct model would never cause coordination issues
That coordination cost should always be fixed by adding more code reviewers to the Pricing service
That a technically clean split can still fail if no single team can own it without needing another team's sign-off
That this is a normal, healthy amount of cross-team coordination for any shared service
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the pitfall: a domain-correct boundary can still generate a real coordination tax if it lacks single-team ownership, so team-ownership needs to be a first-class design constraint alongside domain purity. The model isn't necessarily wrong on domain grounds, more reviewers doesn't fix an ownership problem, and this level of negotiation is exactly the coordination cost the topic frames as a failure mode, not something 'normal and healthy.'
